questions.stem: A fair die is rolled twice. What is the probability that the sum is 7?

options.explanation: The pairs summing to 7 are (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1) — that is 6 pairs out of $6 \times 6 = 36$ equally likely outcomes. So the probability is $6/36 = 1/6$.
The sum ranges from 2 to 12, but the outcomes are not equally likely. There are 36 equally likely outcome pairs, not 11 equally likely sums.
5/36 is the probability of rolling a sum of 6 (or 8). For sum 7, there are 6 favourable pairs, not 5.
There are 6 pairs summing to 7, not 7. Check: (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1).

questions.stem: A test for a rare disease has 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity. The disease affects 0.1% of the population. A person tests positive. What is the approximate probability they have the disease?

options.explanation: Using Bayes: $P(D^+|T^+) = P(T^+|D^+)P(D^+)/P(T^+)$. With $P(D^+)=0.001$, $P(T^+|D^+)=0.99$, $P(T^+|D^-)=0.01$: numerator $\approx 0.00099$; denominator $\approx 0.00099 + 0.00999 \approx 0.01098$. Ratio $\approx 0.09$ or 9%. This counterintuitive result is why screening for rare conditions is tricky.
This ignores the base rate (how rare the disease is). Even a very accurate test will mostly produce false positives when the disease is rare.
This might seem like a sensible default but ignores the actual numbers. Bayes' theorem is required.
This is just the base rate — it ignores the test result entirely.

questions.stem: If $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, then $Z = (X - \mu)/\sigma$ has which distribution?

options.explanation: Standardising shifts the mean to 0 (subtracting $\mu$) and scales the standard deviation to 1 (dividing by $\sigma$). This transformation underlies all standard normal table lookups.
Dividing by $\sigma$ changes the variance to 1, but subtracting $\mu$ also shifts the mean to 0.

options.text: A $t$-distribution with one degree of freedom.
options.explanation: A $t$-distribution arises when the population variance is unknown and estimated from the sample. Here $\sigma$ is known.
$Z^2$ follows a $\chi^2_1$ distribution, but $Z$ itself is standard normal.

questions.stem: The Central Limit Theorem guarantees that, under suitable conditions:

options.text: The distribution of the standardised sample mean $\frac{\bar{X}_n - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$ converges to $N(0,1)$ as $n \to \infty$, regardless of the distribution of the $X_i$.
options.explanation: This is the CLT. The only conditions needed are that the $X_i$ are i.i.d. with finite mean $\mu$ and finite variance $\sigma^2$. The original distribution can be anything.

options.text: The sample mean $\bar{X}_n$ converges to the population mean $\mu$ as $n \to \infty$.
options.explanation: That is the Law of Large Numbers (not the CLT). The LLN says $\bar{X}_n \to \mu$; the CLT says the scaled fluctuations are normal.

options.text: The sum of $n$ normal random variables is normal.
options.explanation: True, but that is a special property of the normal distribution, not the CLT. The CLT applies to non-normal distributions.

options.text: All distributions with large sample size are approximately normal.
options.explanation: It is the distribution of the sample mean (or sum) that becomes approximately normal, not the distribution of individual observations.
